authoredPrompt: This figure is a perspective pictorial schematic of a basic NMR spectrometer, laying out sample, magnet, and signal path in one view. At the center a slender glass tube holding an orange column of sample solution stands upright, tagged "Sample in tube" by a leader line; a green helical coil wraps the tube's midsection between two blue collars. Two cylindrical magnet pole pieces face the coil from either side, the left one lettered S and the right one lettered N. At lower left a beige benchtop unit with knobs, small colored buttons, and a green digital readout showing 9.56 is labeled "Radiofrequency generator", and green leads run from it up to the coil. Blue cables leave the coil to the right and enter a dark gray box with two dials and a green and a red pushbutton, labeled "Detector and amplifier", from which further blue cables climb to a flat-panel monitor at the upper right. The monitor shows a pale blue field crossed by a red baseline carrying several sharp vertical peaks of unequal height. The left-to-right arrangement traces energy from generator to sample to detector to display, letting the reader follow one absorption event to a plotted line. The drawing introduces the instrument in which a strong field aligns 1H and 13C nuclei and swept field strength brings each into resonance separately.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for magnetic field strength: with the radiofrequency irradiation held constant, the learner varies the field between the magnet poles; nuclei in the sample flash as they come into resonance and the monitor adds or emphasizes the matching spectral peak.
- Click for instrument signal path: select the generator, coil, detector, or monitor, and the connected cables and active component highlight in sequence, making the flow from rf irradiation to sample response to amplified spectrum clear.
authoredContext:
The operation of a basic NMR spectrometer is illustrated in the figure. An organic sample is dissolved in a suitable solvent (usually deuteriochloroform, CDCl3, which has no hydrogens) and placed in a thin glass tube between the poles of a magnet. The strong magnetic field causes the 1H and 13C nuclei in the molecule to align in one of the two possible orientations, and the sample is irradiated with rf energy. If the frequency of the rf irradiation is held constant and the strength of the applied magnetic field is varied, each nucleus comes into resonance at a slightly different field strength. A sensitive detector monitors the absorption of rf energy, and its electronic signal is then amplified and displayed as a peak.

Schematic operation of a basic NMR spectrometer. A thin glass tube containing the sample solution is placed between the poles of a strong magnet and irradiated with rf energy.

Schematic diagram of spectrometer shows sample in tube placed between south and north poles. Tube connects to radiofrequency generator (left) and detector and amplifier (right), which further connects to monitor.

NMR spectroscopy differs from IR spectroscopy (another section–another section) in that the timescales of the two techniques are quite different. The absorption of infrared energy by a molecule giving rise to a change in vibrational amplitude is an essentially instantaneous process (about 10–13 s), but the NMR process is much slower (about 10–3 s). This difference in timescales between IR and NMR spectroscopy is analogous to the difference between cameras operating at very fast and very slow shutter speeds. The fast camera (IR) takes an instantaneous picture and freezes the action. If two rapidly interconverting species are present, IR spectroscopy records the spectrum of both. The slow camera (NMR), however, takes a blurred, time-averaged picture. If two species interconverting faster than 103 times per second are present in a sample, NMR records only a single, averaged spectrum, rather than separate spectra of the two discrete species.

discrepancies: Text labels (S, N, component names) are extremely small and illegible compared to the original figure
The digital display on the RF generator shows '8.00' instead of '9.56' and lacks the dark rectangular inset
Labels 'S' and 'N' are floating in front of the magnets rather than printed on their faces
The spectrum peaks on the monitor are drawn as simple triangles instead of the sharp doublet/singlet lines in the source
Cables intersect the instruments awkwardly instead of attaching to specific ports on the panels
evaluation.notes: The 3D models and interactions capture the NMR concept well, but severe label legibility issues and minor styling details detract from faithfulness.
action_items: Increase the font size of all text annotations significantly so they are legible.
Position the 'S' and 'N' labels as flat text or decals directly on the inner faces of the magnets.
Model the RF generator display as a dark inset panel and change the default text to '9.56'.
Refine the red spectrum lines on the monitor to match the sharp vertical needle-like peaks of the source.
